ADClip7.note: The classic Airwindows loudness clipper for dense mixes. Boost pushes into a smart clipper, Soften rounds the clips, and Enhance restores highs and lows lost to clipping. The modes switch between normal, gain-match and clip-only listening.

ADClip8.note: Up to eight stacked ClipOnly2 stages for loudness, with modes from gentle to 'Apocalypse'. Ceiling sets the output peak.

ADClip9.note: The newest ADClip, built on ClipOnly3, which uses noise to hide hard clipping. Boost pushes louder, Match level-compensates so you can judge the tone honestly, and ClipOnly lets you hear just what's clipped.

ADT.note: Two short delay taps for ADT, fixed flanging and thickening, like the Abbey Road double-tracking trick. Each tap's level knob goes negative to flip its polarity, which changes which frequencies the comb filter cancels.

AQuickVoiceClip.note: Softens and darkens voice recordings that were hard-clipped on capture, like screams into a gaming headset.

Acceleration.note: An acceleration limiter, the kind used in vinyl mastering to protect the cutting head. It tames edge and harshness while keeping apparent brightness.

Acceleration2.note: An updated Acceleration that works at high sample rates and goes further. It glues the top end without dulling it, and Chris says it's not an emulation of any gear.

Air.note: The original Air: boosts or cuts at 22k, 15k and 11k. It only behaves right at 44.1k, so use Air2 otherwise.

Air2.note: Three treble bands (Hiss, Glitter, Air) and a Silk control inspired by the Neve Portico Silk transformer, which adds second-harmonic warmth. Center is flat on the three bands.

Air3.note: An experimental air-band EQ using a Kalman filter. It splits the sound into 'air' and 'ground' (body) so you can rebalance them. Center is unity on both.

Air4.note: Air3 plus a high-frequency limiter, so you can push air without spiky overslew. It's about getting a bright record the way analog media naturally limited the extreme top.

AngleEQ.note: A very colorful, phasey three-band EQ that became the tone stack in PointyGuitar and ChimeyGuitar. Chris says not to use it as a main EQ.

AngleFilter.note: A synth-style resonant filter built from AngleEQ's odd, colorful filter type.

Apicolypse.note: Chris's old API-style console color adder, re-released unchanged. A precursor to BussColors.

AtmosphereBuss.note: The mix-bus half of the Console5-family Atmosphere system: multi-stage slew clipping that glues and tames digital highs and adds a sense of acoustic distance. Use it with AtmosphereChannel on each track. Like all Console systems, channels feed the bus at unity gain.

AtmosphereChannel.note: The track half of Atmosphere. Put it on every channel, mix with its input knob instead of faders, and put AtmosphereBuss on the mix bus.

Aura.note: An odd resonant lowpass EQ that shapes tone with a glowing resonance instead of a plain cut.

AutoPan.note: An auto-panner for slow, organic stereo movement, with phase and width controls.

AverMatrix.note: Stacks averaging filters into a full lowpass-style EQ with a natural, slightly comb-filtered roll-off. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Average.note: A simple averaging lowpass. Its gentle, slightly combed darkening sounds natural and underrated.

Balanced.note: Takes a balanced XLR signal that arrives as a stereo pair, sums it to mono and lets you trim it in clean 6 dB steps. Inspired by the Teenage Engineering TX-6.

BassAmp.note: A blend of bass amp voices: bright, clean mids, a woolly 'dub' bass and a trashy sub-octave. Treat the sub as a special effect.

BassDrive.note: Chris's take on the rackmount SansAmp Bass DI (RBI). The EQ bands are voiced oddly and include overdrive, so treat them as tone colors rather than clean EQ.

BassKit.note: Clean, controllable centered bass reinforcement (ToTape-style head bump) plus a deep sub fill, made for the mix bus and mastering. You need real subs or SubsOnly to hear the sub output. Both outputs go negative to flip polarity.

Baxandall.note: Classic hi-fi bass and treble shelves: broad, musical, and bit-transparent at zero. A go-to general EQ.

Baxandall2.note: A stripped-down, more powerful Baxandall with ±24 dB range.

Baxandall3.note: Mixes parts of both earlier Baxandalls for unusual tone colors that Chris admits most people don't reach for.

Beam.note: A wordlength reducer (dither alternative) that steers the noise toward more sonority and focus rather than darkness. Use it as the last plugin when exporting to 16 or 24 bit.

BezEQ.note: A strange three-band shelving EQ built on Bezier-curve reconstruction. It's unlike any normal EQ. The two unnamed knobs set the crossover points.

BezEQ2.note: BezEQ with its bugs fixed. A subtle, slippery three-band shelving EQ.

BezEQ3.note: Four unified Bezier EQ bands with sweepable frequencies and zero latency, designed with a Console in mind. Center is flat on the gains.

BeziComp.note: An experimental compressor that shapes gain with a Bezier curve, so it doesn't alias. The good settings can be fussy, and extreme settings get weird.

BigAmp.note: The widest-ranging of Chris's amp sims. It can sound fairly normal, and the knobs also go well past realistic for layering and odd sounds.

Biquad.note: A standard digital filter done with extra precision so it sounds less plasticky and DAW-like. Choose lowpass, highpass, bandpass or notch. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Biquad2.note: A biquad filter made smooth enough to sweep and automate like a synth filter, with very high resonance available. It can freak out at the extremes.

BiquadDouble.note: Two biquads in series for twice the slope before resonance, run through Chris's internal console for a deeper tone.

BiquadHiLo.note: The high and low cut filters from ConsoleX on their own. Zero on either knob switches that filter off.

BiquadNonLin.note: A lowpass or bandpass filter whose frequency shifts with level, like the voltage-sensitive ceramic capacitors in Capacitor2. It gives analog-feeling, nonlinear filtering.

BiquadOneHalf.note: An experimental interleaved biquad. Set the frequency twice as high as you would on Biquad, and it tops out at a quarter of Nyquist.

BiquadPlus.note: Biquad with zipper-noise smoothing, so it's safe to sweep, automate or modulate.

BiquadStack.note: One parametric bell built from stacked biquads. Chris made it while studying what makes SSL channel EQ bands special, as a test for ConsoleX.

BiquadTriple.note: Three biquads in series for even steeper slopes before resonance.

BitDualPan.note: Separate volume and pan for left and right, using near-bit-shift gain for very clean level changes.

BitGlitter.note: Old digital sampler grit and glitter. It's dirtier than DeRez, the way vintage samplers actually behaved.

BitShiftGain.note: The cleanest possible gain change: bit-shifts in exact 6 dB steps, which in floating point lose nothing.

BitShiftPan.note: Volume and pan done only with bit shifts, for lossless level moves.

Bite.note: Adds a harsh midrange edge (more treble at high sample rates), or removes it below center.

BlockParty.note: A Chris compressor crossed with OneCornerClip. It acts like a somewhat distorted analog limiter with no lookahead, so attacks get mangled in a musical way.

BrassRider.note: A trick for metal drum overheads: it rides cymbal wash down so the kit punches through. Chris made it for one friend.

BrightAmbience.note: A pile of prime-spaced delay taps that makes a metallic, very bright gated halo rather than a believable room. The wet signal runs hot, so mostly-dry settings work best.

BrightAmbience2.note: Bright Lexicon-style sparkle and slapback without a long tail. Good for 80s gated drums, blurry dub slaps and glitter on vocals at low levels. It also spreads mono sources into stereo.

BrightAmbience3.note: The latest BrightAmbience. Tone and length stay consistent at high sample rates, it's slightly darker, and the feedback turns it into vintage-feeling blurred echoes.

BuildATPDF.note: A toolkit for designing dither noise by weighting ten neighboring samples. Chris made DoublePaul this way: set the middle two to -1 and +1, then shape the rest by ear. Center is zero on each.

BussColors4.note: Chris's long-running console emulations: eight dynamic colors (Dark, Rock, Lush, Vibe, Holo, Punch, Steel, Tube) based on real console impulses.

ButterComp.note: Chris's gentlest compressor and a cult favorite. Very subtle and smooth, not for hard control.

ButterComp2.note: The improved ButterComp, with a bug fixed so its interleaved compressors really work, and an output control added. It's smooth, subtle glue.

C5RawBuss.note: The original Console5 bus algorithm with optional gentle DC suppression. Pair it with C5RawChannel.

C5RawChannel.note: The original Console5 channel algorithm with optional gentle DC suppression. Pair it with C5RawBuss.

CStrip.note: The original Airwindows channel strip: lossless three-band EQ with sweepable bands, high and low cuts, gate, compressor and a time-lag delay.

CStrip2.note: A full channel strip: three-band EQ with sweepable treble and bass, Capacitor high and low cuts, and the CStrip compressor.

Cabs.note: A guitar speaker cabinet with six cab types, cabinet size, mic off-axis position and room loudness. The speaker coloration can be pushed up or pulled back to almost nothing.

Cabs2.note: A speaker-cab tone built from deliberately phasey filters, with a lowpass and a highpass. Chris liked it enough to build it into a console channel.

Calibre.note: An old Character plugin with a steely tone. Push Character far enough and the bass cancels, which makes it an odd tone control.

Cans.note: Makes headphone mixing feel like a room. Choose a room, then set diffusion, damping and crossfeed. Put it on the master only while monitoring.

CansAW.note: Cans with Chris's own tuned room presets. Pick a seat position. For monitoring only.

Capacitor.note: A new kind of lowpass and highpass that behaves like a real capacitor filter, gentle and analog-feeling.

Capacitor2.note: Capacitor with modeled ceramic-cap behavior, where capacitance drops under voltage so the filter moves with level, for extra analog mojo.

Chamber.note: A feedforward reverb where every internal delay is the golden ratio of the next, giving a dense, chamber-like space.

Chamber2.note: Chamber modified into a feedforward reverb that doubles as a blurry delay with a glitchy top.

Channel4.note: Console-channel tone coloring with Neve, API or SSL voicings: saturation, a calibrated slew clipper and a highpass. Pair it with Console on the bus.

Channel5.note: Channel for 2018, with new subtleties and an output control.

Channel6.note: Channel using the Spiral saturation algorithm.

Channel7.note: Channel with better slew clipping at high sample rates, and drive that blends between Channel5 and 6 behavior.

Channel8.note: Channel7 with Capacitor2 and Slew3 updates. A subtle analogifier with Neve, API or SSL voicing.

Channel9.note: Channel8 plus ultrasonic filtering and new Teac and Mackie 'low end' voicings. A subtle console-channel analogifier: drive, highpass and slew clipping.

ChannelX.note: Channel9's layout with a set of wild experimental voicings instead of the classic consoles.

ChimeyDeluxe.note: Ten intense EQ bands with compression stages between each one, built on PointyDeluxe. It's extreme and is meant to go into Cabs2 or an IR before it sounds nice. Each knob boosts or cuts one band, and center is neutral.

ChimeyGuitar.note: PointyGuitar's tone stack and cab, but the amp squashes instead of distorting, so you get chimey, compressed cleans.

ChimeyGuitar2.note: A more intense ChimeyGuitar with a stronger compressor. Chris warns it can pop and blow up at bad settings, so keep the output down while dialing it in.

Chorus.note: One moving delay tap against the dry signal, with smooth analog-feeling interpolation. Set the mix to full wet for vibrato.

ChorusEnsemble.note: Like Chorus but with a bank of taps for a thicker, more lush ensemble. Good on pads and background parts. Extreme settings can sound broken on purpose.

ChromeOxide.note: An experimental tape sound: saturated lows plus highs that warble with random delay, adjustable by bias.

Cider.note: An old Character plugin. Chris says it 'sounds kinda like an MCI console?' and left little more description.

ClearCoat.note: Seventeen dual-mono bright ambiences in one plugin. It adds sparkle and air that stays tied to the source rather than a lingering tail. Chris uses it on his own album mixes.

ClipOnly2.note: Chris's mastering-grade clipper. It never touches samples below 0 dBFS and only smooths the edges going into and out of clipping, so clips lose their grit. Leave it at the end of a chain as a safety. No controls.

ClipOnly3.note: ClipOnly2 that can go harder, hiding the sound of clipping under a little noise, an idea borrowed from bass-music loudness tricks. Unclipped samples still pass untouched. No controls.

ClipSoftly.note: ClipOnly2's smoothing applied to the softest possible clip curve. It works as a soft safety clipper and a gentle saturation. No controls.

CloudCoat.note: Seventeen allpass blur effects in one plugin, a darker sibling of ClearCoat. It smears sounds into bloom-like clouds.

Coils.note: Transformer saturation that softens only the extreme highs and lows and leaves the mids, shaped after a Neve transformer response. Very subtle.

Coils2.note: Coils with a Cheapness control that can push the transformer from subtle to wrecked.

Cojones.note: Tracks the waveform's trajectory and heightens or softens different parts: breathiness, aggression ('cojones') and body. Center is neutral on each. It's the seed of Chris's StudioTan quantizers.

Compresaturator.note: Fades between compressing and soft clipping, with a springy, dynamic feel. It's more of a stem or bus compressor than a peak limiter.

Console0Buss.note: Chris's most radical, minimalist Console system, with volume and pan. He says you'll either hear what it's about or you won't. Pair it with Console0Channel.

Console0Channel.note: The track half of Console Zero, with volume and pan. Pair it with Console0Buss.

Console4Buss.note: The original Airwindows in-the-box mix system. Channel plugins on every track feed this bus plugin at unity, so tracks saturate against each other like an analog bus. No controls.

Console4Channel.note: The track half of Console4. Put it on every track and pair it with Console4Buss. No controls.

Console5Buss.note: A richer, warmer Console using Density/PurestDrive-style math. Pair it with Console5Channel.

Console5Channel.note: The track half of Console5. Pair it with Console5Buss.

Console5DarkCh.note: A darker variant of the Console5 channel. Use it on tracks that feed Console5Buss.

Console6Buss.note: A more intense Console built on an inverse-square encode and decode. It saturates at lower levels than earlier Consoles. Pair it with Console6Channel.

Console6Channel.note: The track half of Console6. Pair it with Console6Buss.

Console7Buss.note: The Console7 mix bus with anti-alias filtering and saturation curves tied to the master level. Channel plugins on every track feed it at unity, so tracks interact and saturate like an analog bus.

Console7Cascade.note: A drop-in Console7Channel with five filtered stages of saturation, for slamming the console hard.

Console7Channel.note: Put it on every track and use its fader instead of the DAW fader, feeding Console7Buss. The saturation curve changes with fader position, and about 0.77 is unity.

Console7Crunch.note: Like Console7Cascade, but voiced for more edge and grit.

Console8BussHype.note: A brighter, sparklier replacement for Console8BussIn. Console8 runs as Channel → Submix → Bus, with an In and an Out plugin at each stage. No controls.

Console8BussIn.note: Console8 adds subtle analog-style texture and depth, and runs as Channel → Submix → Bus, each with an In and Out plugin. Put this first on the mix bus and Console8BussOut last. No controls.

Console8BussOut.note: The end of the Console8 mix-bus pair. The fader sets the bus level.

Console8ChannelHype.note: A brighter, sparklier replacement for Console8ChannelIn. No controls.

Console8ChannelIn.note: Goes first on each track in a Console8 setup, with Console8ChannelOut last. No controls.

Console8ChannelOut.note: Goes last on each track in a Console8 setup. Mix with this fader instead of the DAW fader.

Console8LiteBuss.note: A simplified Console8 for a plain tracks-into-mix-bus setup, with no submix stage needed. Pair it with Console8LiteChannel.

Console8LiteChannel.note: The track half of Console8 Lite. Mix with this fader and pair it with Console8LiteBuss.

Console8SubHype.note: A brighter, sparklier replacement for Console8SubIn. No controls.

Console8SubIn.note: Goes first on a submix bus in a Console8 setup, with Console8SubOut last. No controls.

Console8SubOut.note: Goes last on a Console8 submix bus. The fader sets the submix level.

Console9Buss.note: The summing engine from ConsoleX on its own, with pan and fader. Pair it with Console9Channel.

Console9Channel.note: The track half of Console9. Pan and mix here, and pair it with Console9Buss.

ConsoleLABuss.note: Chris's take on the Quad Eight, the 70s LA console behind Steely Dan-era records. Pair it with ConsoleLAChannel.

ConsoleLAChannel.note: A Quad Eight-style channel with its three-band EQ, pan and fader. Pair it with ConsoleLABuss. Center is flat on the EQ knobs.

ConsoleMCBuss.note: Chris's first, brighter take on the MCI console that replaced his analog desk. Pair it with ConsoleMCChannel. ConsoleMD is the later version.

ConsoleMCChannel.note: An MCI-style channel with treble, a sweepable mid peak, bass, pan and fader. Pair it with ConsoleMCBuss.

ConsoleMDBuss.note: The refined MCI console emulation that replaced Chris's analog mixer. Pair it with ConsoleMDChannel.

ConsoleMDChannel.note: The refined MCI channel: treble, a sweepable mid peak, bass, pan and fader, with the tone shaping of a classic MCI desk. Pair it with ConsoleMDBuss.

ContentHideD.note: Mutes audio except for short glimpses. Chris made it for showing music on YouTube without giving away the whole track. No controls.

CreamCoat.note: A Swiss-army reverb built on ClearCoat's seventeen spaces, with soft undersampling for a creamy tone, plus feedback and pre-delay.

Creature.note: A new kind of saturation that applies a sine curve to slew (rate of change) instead of level. It softens and thickens in an unusual way. Inverted, it removes what it would add.

CrickBass.note: Stereo-in bass tone in the style of Chris Squire's Rickenbacker. Feed it the neck pickup on the left and the bridge pickup on the right. The bridge side gets the grind and the neck side stays clean.

CrunchCoat.note: ClearCoat's ambiences run through crunchy undersampling, like a cheap 80s digital reverb.

CrunchyGrooveWear.note: GrooveWear with more edge and distortion, like a worn, slightly crunchy record.

Crystal.note: The first Character reissue: tone shaping and soft clipping for the bus. One user's favorite bus plugin.

DCVoltage.note: Outputs a DC voltage for modular gear. Never use it on speakers: on a DC-coupled system it can blow woofers.

Dark.note: A wordlength reducer that follows the waveform's trajectory, giving a blacker, quieter background with highs slightly suppressed. Use it last, when exporting.

DarkNoise.note: Generates bassier, more midrangey noise directly, for sound design.

Dattorro.note: The state-variable resonant lowpass from Donut on its own. A smooth synth-style filter.

DeBess.note: Chris's best de-esser. It detects real esses by their fast back-and-forth slew and ignores other bright material. The Sense knob lets you hear only what it's removing.

DeBez.note: Bezier-based sample-rate and bit reduction for retro sampler textures. A cousin of DeRez and HipCrush.

DeCrackle.note: Finds clicks and vinyl crackle and removes them, with a surface-noise control. Made for cleaning up records.

DeEss.note: Detects esses by slew-rate behavior rather than frequency, so it triggers hard on esses and not on other bright sounds. Turn it up until you clearly hear it working, then set the depth.

DeHiss.note: A filtering gate that darkens quiet passages whenever there's no loud treble. It was made for noisy USB mics.

DeNoise.note: A multiband gate: raise a band's threshold and that band gates out when quiet. Zero on every band means no gating. It can also be pushed into a wild effect.

DeRez.note: A continuous sample-rate and bit crusher with fractional settings. Smooth rather than gritty.

DeRez2.note: DeRez with a hardness control for more authentic retro digital hardware tones.

DeRez3.note: A rethought DeRez for old-school lo-fi digital, like vintage reverbs and samplers.

DeRez4.note: Chris's refined retro digital tone: crushing with brightness and bass controls, good at the things vintage digital gear did well.

DeRez5.note: DeRez4 plus new derez modes (trim and square). Set Square to 0 and Trim to 1 to get DeRez4.

Deckwrecka.note: Fattens and dirties up beats. Made for composer Alan Gold (Agzilla).

Density.note: Chris's classic smooth saturation, using a sine transfer curve with no grit. Settings below the default go into anti-saturation, which un-thickens and opens up a sound. The highpass keeps bass out of the saturation.

Density2.note: Older Density code with a different tone that people asked to have back.

Density3.note: The refined Density. Sine-based overdrive with a gentle highpass so heavy bass doesn't over-saturate. The best Density to start with.

Desk.note: Classic subtle Airwindows analog modeling: glues and thickens with about 30 dB of headroom, like a real console channel. No controls.

Desk4.note: Tunable analog-console color: overdrive, high-frequency choke and power-supply sag, not a clone of any one desk.

DigitalBlack.note: A quick gate for tightening staccato DI tracks like palm-muted guitar or bass. It cuts hard and fast instead of fading.

Dirt.note: A softer, tubier version of Edge with less gain. The low and high cut filters match Edge's, so you can switch between them.

Discontapeity.note: Discontinuity's air-loudness model combined with TapeHack's tape overdrive, on one knob.

Discontinuity.note: Models air behaving nonlinearly at intense loudness, which Chris thinks is part of why DAWs sound 'too perfect'. Set how loud 0 dBFS would be in the room.

Disintegrate.note: Discontinuity pushed into total unreality: it models air compressing asymmetrically at loud levels, then layers and buffers it. You set how loud 0 dBFS would be in the real world.

Distance.note: Mimics high frequencies being absorbed by air over distance, to push a sound or reverb farther back.

Distance2.note: Distance crossed with Atmosphere. It's very good at making drums huge, pounding and far away.

Distance3.note: Distance plus Discontinuity's model of air compressing at loud levels, for distant and huge.

Distortion.note: Several smooth, slightly dark Airwindows distortion curves in one plugin, tuned to behave well at high sample rates.

DitherFloat.note: A demonstration of floating-point truncation that can also dither to 32-bit float. Chris says it's not for mixes.

DitherMeDiskers.note: A dark, deep quantizer for 16-bit output. Strictly speaking it isn't a dither, but it competes with the best ones. No controls.

DitherMeTimbers.note: The 24-bit version of DitherMeDiskers. No controls.

Ditherbox.note: Nearly every Airwindows dither in one plugin, in 16 and 24-bit versions, plus monitoring tools for hearing the noise floor.

Donut.note: An envelope-following resonant filter in the spirit of J Dilla's filtered sounds. Chris says it's not a clone of any one effect. Frequency and resonance move with the input's dynamics.

DoublePaul.note: PaulDither taken further, with the noise pushed even higher in pitch. It's for people who want traditional TPDF behavior rather than Chris's boutique dithers. No controls.

Doublelay.note: Pitch-shifted stereo doubling with separate left and right delays and feedback. It thickens vocals, makes 'echojam' pitch-shifted echoes, or with feedback up smears into pitch trails.

Drive.note: Laid out like Density but only for slamming. It has more grit and attitude than Density's smoothness.

DrumSlam.note: Heavy tape-style processing that pushes drums into dense, punchy saturation. It splits the signal into bands and drives them like slammed tape.

DubCenter.note: DubSub with the bass and sub outputs kept mono, the way vinyl and PA systems want them. It's the extreme version of BassKit.

DubPlate.note: Ruthless dubplate-style mastering for electronic music. Chris used it to put out a record. No controls.

DubPlate2.note: An in-the-box mastering house for electronic music, with input, treble and bass. Center is unity on each.

DubSub.note: A full bass toolkit: a presence-style treble grind, a crossover, a ToTape-style bass bump and a sub-octave section, each with its own drive, voicing and level. Levels go negative to flip polarity.

DubSub2.note: The tape-machine head bump on its own: a saturating low-frequency resonance like the one in ToTape, now tamed and tunable.

Dubly.note: The encode side of the famous 70s tape noise-reduction trick (filter, compress 2:1, add back) used on its own for vibe and atmosphere. Chris doesn't name the brand, but the name gives it away.

Dubly2.note: The full noise-reduction loop: encode, drive the tape, then decode. Encode and decode deliberately mismatched is a big part of 70s record sound. It's a component of ToTape7.

Dubly3.note: Dubly refined into a simple tilt: more encode brightens and compresses the top, more decode darkens it.

DustBunny.note: Unpredictable distorted crackle, like dust stuck under a turntable needle. It started as a happy bug.

Dynamics.note: The compressor and gate from CStrip, combined into one dynamics stage. Transparent, or punchy with the speed cranked.

Dynamics2.note: The ConsoleX compressor and gate with BeziComp's artifact-free Bezier curves. Threshold at full means no compression.

Dynamics3.note: A Bezier compressor with vari-mu behavior, which modulates the wet blend as well as level. Chris says it's not a Fairchild emulation. Below center on the last knob it becomes an expander.

Dyno.note: Like Mojo, but it makes things more intense instead of louder.

EQ.note: The EQ section of CStrip: a lossless three-band EQ (bit-identical when flat), sweepable treble and bass, and a highpass and lowpass.

EdIsDim.note: The second half of a mid/side sandwich. Put MidSide first, your plugins in between, then EdIsDim to return to left/right.

Edge.note: Seven hard-clipping stages with steep anti-alias filtering between them. Bright with very high gain, good for in-the-box guitars.

Elation.note: Built from LA-2A impulses, but Chris says it's not really an LA-2A and doesn't properly compress. It's a color, not a leveler.

ElectroHat.note: Uses the input as a trigger to generate crude electronic hi-hat noise, with six hat types.

Elliptical.note: An elliptical EQ that highpasses only the side channel, so low end collapses to mono like a vinyl cutting EQ.

Energy.note: Eight very narrow boosts and cuts locked to fractions of the sample rate, from top-end hiss down to high-mid snarl. Center is flat on each band. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Energy2.note: Energy with undersampling so the bands land in the same places at high sample rates. Center is flat on each band.

Ensemble.note: A quirky multi-tap thickener that ended up flangey and small rather than a lush pad maker. Use it for character rather than as a standard chorus.

EveryConsole.note: The core summing math of a dozen Console versions with no tone shaping or filtering, so you can mix and match or compare them. Pick the same type for channel and bus.

EverySlew.note: Slew, GoldenSlew and PlatinumSlew combined, with halo and inverted modes. It's very flexible and has no clear presets, so use GoldenSlew or PlatinumSlew if you just want tamer highs.

EveryTrim.note: Every basic stereo trim in one plugin: left, right, mid, side and master, each ±12 dB.

Exciter.note: The classic exciter effect heard on records like Steely Dan's The Royal Scam: generated upper harmonics for presence. Chris says it isn't a clone of any brand.

Facet.note: A new kind of hard clip that bends the wave at a knee instead of flattening it, for a distinct edgy distortion.

FastDistance.note: An ultra-light distance lowpass Chris made for game engines. It's cheap enough to put on every sound.

FatEQ.note: Balances four bands with saturation density instead of plain gain, so loud and quiet parts change differently. Above center thickens and below center thins.

FathomFive.note: A cross between an EQ and a bass amp that adds deep bass bloom and an optional sub-octave. Chris designed it for a bass aux bus with Console4.

FinalClip.note: A ClipOnly2-based clipper set to clip at +6 dB to suit Final Cut Pro's gain staging. It's mainly for video work. No controls.

FireAmp.note: A bright, loud, midrangey tube-style amp with a high-mid howl and not much low chug. Chris calls it 'sort of Marshally'. It's also good layered under other guitars.

Flipity.note: Flips the polarity of left, right or both, and swaps channels, in every combination.

Floor.note: Adds harmonics tied to the bass so you hear a lower octave that isn't really there, similar in idea to Waves MaxxBass. Chris calls it a 'don't do this' plugin, so use it sparingly.

Flutter.note: The wobble from ToTape6 on its own, for unsteady tape movement without the rest of a tape sim.

Flutter2.note: The newer flutter from ToTape7, with depth and speed controls.

Focus.note: Distorts only a resonant band and leaves the rest clean, bringing out clarity. Five distortion modes, from subtle to aggressive.

Fracture.note: A sine-based wavefolder like Buchla-style West Coast synthesis. Drive pushes into the folds, and Fracture sets how many folds before hard clipping.

Fracture2.note: A more extreme wavefolder. Drive at 0.1 is unity, Fracture goes exponential before folding, and Threshold sets the fold point.

FromTape.note: A minimalist, cleaner tape emulation: ToTape without the head bump, for subtle tape glue.

Galactic.note: A super-wide, detuned space reverb designed for pads and ambient. 'Replace' controls how much new sound replaces the tail versus sustaining it.

Galactic2.note: A redesigned Galactic with drive into the tank, sustain and darkening. A different flavor rather than a replacement.

Galactic3.note: Exactly Galactic with better undersampling. It's the one to use.

GalacticVibe.note: The quadrature stereo vibrato from Galactic reverb, broken out as a chorus-like widener.

Gatelope.note: A gate that lets highs and lows close at different speeds. It was made to gate tom mics against cymbal bleed while keeping the low sustain.

GlitchShifter.note: A gnarly, up-front pitch shifter that jumps between loops instead of blending, so it glitches and has personality. Semitone steps, fine trim and feedback for climbing pitch.

GoldenSlew.note: A chain of progressively tighter slew clippers that darkens highs with a slightly edgy character instead of plain dulling.

Golem.note: Blends a stereo track of two mics on a guitar cab down to mono, with balance, a time offset to align them, and polarity options.

GrindAmp.note: A heavier amp with some beef for chugging rhythm parts. Chris calls it 'sort of Mesa-y'. The mix knob blends both the dry amp and the dry guitar back in.

Gringer.note: Full-wave rectification like the Dan Armstrong Green Ringer pedal: a ring-mod-ish octave-up grind. Chris warns it's deliberately unmusical. No controls.

GrooveWear.note: Scrubs highs off mechanically, the way a stylus wears a groove. A smooth, natural roll-off.

GuitarConditioner.note: The midrange push of a Tube Screamer without the squish and blur, built from Slew and Highpass in parallel. Put it before an amp sim. No controls.

HardVacuum.note: Classic Airwindows tube-style saturation. Warmth adds second harmonic, and Aura adds a strange airy phase-y sheen.

HermeTrim.note: EveryTrim with very fine ±1.5 dB adjustments, for mastering.

Hermepass.note: A clean mastering highpass with only cutoff and a continuous slope (up to six poles). It was made for Hermetech Mastering and deliberately has no frequency labels, so set it by ear.

HighGlossDither.note: A hybrid of dither and truncation that keeps some of truncation's glossy character. Chris calls it an unnatural science experiment. No controls.

HighImpact.note: Distorted grit and attack without adding thickness. Good for making something cut through rather than bloom.

Highpass.note: A mixing highpass with tight or loose tone shaping that pulls sounds toward a retro, midrangey vibe. The more you filter, the more it also softens the extreme top.

Highpass2.note: Highpass with a continuously variable slope from one to four poles, plus loose/tight tone shaping.

HipCrush.note: The de-rez section of ConsoleH: three EQ bands that each crush bits on their own, for new hip-hop and lo-fi textures.

Holt.note: A resonant, synth-like lowpass built on a forecasting method from accounting (Holt's method), tuned for bass frequencies.

Holt2.note: Holt extended into a bass-cabinet-like resonant lowpass. Chris calls it 'like Aura for bass'.

Hombre.note: Very short delays that act like a reflecting panel next to the mic. Chris built it chasing the ZZ Top / Terry Manning guitar texture. It thickens and colors rather than echoing.

Huge.note: Adds odd harmonics for smooth, mellow saturation that turns square-wave dirty as you push.

Hull.note: A filter built on a stock-market moving-average method. The Bright knob turns it from a lowpass (left) into a highpass (right).

Hull2.note: The pristine three-band EQ behind ConsoleLA's high band, with no saturation or mojo. Center is unity on each band.

Hype.note: A treble-softening experiment from Console8 that went wrong and became an aural exciter. No controls.

Hypersoft.note: A soft clipper whose knee sharpens as you push, with multiple stages and a brightness control.

HypersonX.note: An anti-aliasing filter for high-sample-rate mixes with selectable stage Q, for building your own console-style filtering between nonlinear plugins.

Hypersonic.note: Like Ultrasonic but steeper with a higher cutoff, so it shouldn't soften the extreme top. Put it between saturating plugins at high sample rates to cut aliasing. No controls.

Infinity.note: A matrix reverb that can sustain and layer sounds forever, like a freeze effect.

Infinity2.note: Infinity with more tone shaping and a feedback control that acts as a kill switch for the endless tail.

Inflamer.note: Chris's take on the two waveshapers believed to be inside the Oxford Inflator, improved his way.

Infrasonic.note: A very steep, clean highpass that removes DC and subsonic rumble. It's the low-end twin of Ultrasonic. No controls.

Interstage.note: A subtle, sophisticated analog-style stage that slightly band-limits and softens, like signal passing between analog stages. No controls.

IronOxide5.note: The heavily colored, bandpassy Airwindows tape sim, with separate high and low tape speeds, flutter and noise. For slamming and aggressive color.

IronOxideClassic.note: The original, purer Iron Oxide: sweet tape saturation without flutter, noise or grit.

IronOxideClassic2.note: IronOxideClassic updated for high sample rates and aliasing control.

Isolator.note: A steep, crossover-style filter for DJ sweeps: high and low knobs set how much of each side passes, which also gives shelving. Frequency at full is bypass.

Isolator2.note: An even steeper Isolator with smoothing for automation and a resonance boost to put an edge on sweeps.

Isolator3.note: A one-knob DJ filter: center is full range, left lowpasses and right highpasses. Q narrows it toward a band.

Kalman.note: A GPS-derived Kalman predictor used as a filter. Wet gives the smooth predicted lows, and inverted gives the leftover highs. Odd but useful.

LRConvolve.note: Multiplies the left channel by the right and back, a ring-mod-like mangler for two different sources. No controls.

LRConvolve3.note: Uses one channel to gate the other, roughly or smoothly. Pick which side controls.
LRConvolve3.t: Gate one channel by the other

LRFlipTimer.note: Swaps left and right every 1 to 10 minutes, for checking a mix's balance with fresh ears.

LeadAmp.note: A clear, penetrating, vocal-sounding lead amp that leans toward the Vox side.

LeftoMono.note: Copies the left channel to both sides losslessly. Use it when only the left side of a stereo input has your signal. No controls.

LilAmp.note: Low gain, loud and articulate like a little practice amp. Good for Stonesy rhythm guitar, leads, or turning a snare into a confined whack.

Logical4.note: Chris's classic 2-bus compressor, made to be transparent and solid on the mix bus. The name hints at the SSL bus comp tradition.

Longhand.note: An experimental sine-based soft clipper. The default input is normalized so it doesn't wavefold too far.

Loud.note: Modeled on air itself breaking up at extreme levels (tractor pulls, rocket launches). It can be slammed absurdly hard and stays huge rather than fizzy.

Lowpass.note: A mixing lowpass that deepens tone and leaves a gloss, with soft or hard tone shaping.

Lowpass2.note: A fixed Lowpass that opens fully at any sample rate, plus a variable one-to-four pole slope.

Luxor.note: A Character plugin built from Manley impulses. Chris says it doesn't sound like any Manley. Try it like an amp sim.

MSFlipTimer.note: Switches between stereo and mono every 1 to 10 minutes, for checking mono compatibility.

MV.note: A dual-mono reverb built on the trick inside the old Alesis Midiverb, which used half-gain allpasses because it had no multiplier. Lo-fi in character but made at full quality.

MV2.note: MV adapted so it sounds the same at high sample rates. Use this version over MV.

MackEQ.note: Mackity (the pre-VLZ Mackie 1202 input stage) with its treble and bass shelves added, for overdriving kicks and bass the way people abused those mixers.

Mackity.note: An emulation of the pre-VLZ Mackie 1202 input stage, plugged halfway into the insert point the way people did for color.

Mastering.note: Kalman-filter multiband mastering: Glue (high-frequency control), Scope, Skronk and Girth to rebalance treble, mids and bass, plus drive and dither. Center is neutral on the middle knobs.

Mastering2.note: Mastering plus an elliptical EQ (side-channel bass cut) at the top for vinyl-style mono lows.

MatrixVerb.note: A wildly adjustable Householder-matrix reverb with modulation and a 'flavor' cross-mod for odd colors.

Melt.note: Moving, filtered delay taps that wobble in pitch, tone and level at once. Settings range from a chorus to a strange retro ambience.

MidAmp.note: A loud clean combo like a Twin, with wide EQ range. It also dirties up bass and drums nicely.

MidSide.note: The first half of a mid/side sandwich. It turns left/right into mid/side, and EdIsDim turns it back.

MoNoam.note: Quick switches for mono, mid-only, side-only and similar listening checks.

Mojo.note: A happy-accident saturator that makes things bigger and louder at once.

Monitoring.note: A last-on-the-bus mix-check suite: subs only, slew only, peaks only, mono, side, headphone crossfeed, phone and car-style speakers, plus 16 or 24-bit dither.

Monitoring2.note: Monitoring with Dark as the wordlength reducer.

Monitoring3.note: Monitoring with TenNines into Dark as the wordlength reducer.

MultiBandDistortion.note: An old, gnarly sound-wrecker that splits highs and lows and distorts each separately. Closer to OTT-style slammed effects than Chris's usual natural tone.

NCSeventeen.note: Chris's 'loudenator-killer': a soft clipper whose clipped energy drives a harmonic filter. Dirty and loud.

NaturalizeDither.note: Deterministic dither using Benford's-law 'realness' per sample. Listeners often rate it best: no tonal color, and a quiet noise that seems to vanish. No controls.

Neverland.note: Chris's 2007 Neve emulation from the Character collection, re-released exactly as it was.

Nikola.note: An audio Tesla coil, originally an April Fools' plugin. Low voltage is bright and airy, high voltage roars. It's not supposed to sound nice.

NodeDither.note: A TPDF dither with a delay offset, like a 'dither flanger'. It can reproduce the PaulDither and TapeDither settings.

Noise.note: Chris's deep brownian noise oscillator, driven by the input's dynamics to reinforce sounds like kicks with shaped noise.

NonlinearSpace.note: A reverb with filters and space simulation inside the loops, so it blends into a mix. Nonlinearity makes loud parts livelier or deader.

NotJustAnotherCD.note: Chris's top wordlength reducer for 16-bit/CD output: a noise-shaped take on Naturalize with no randomness. No controls.

NotJustAnotherDither.note: Chris's recommended final-output dither at 24 bit. Choose 16 or 24-bit, plus an optional lo-fi DeRez.

OneCornerClip.note: A full-bandwidth clipper that curves into the clip over several samples and snaps out of it, moving the clip energy lower so it sounds brutal rather than gritty. Positive and negative thresholds are set separately.

OrbitKick.note: A virtual SubKick (the NS10 woofer hung in front of a kick). The kick triggers a generated sub tone, which you blend in for low-end weight.

Overheads.note: Compresses only part of the sound using a delay trick instead of filters. On overheads it squashes the drums and leaves the cymbals alone.

PDBuss.note: Console5 summing with a PurestDrive saturation stage built in. Pair it with PDChannel.

PDChannel.note: The track half of PD Console, with its own PurestDrive saturation. Pair it with PDBuss.

Pafnuty.note: A Chebyshev shaper that adds or subtracts exact harmonics from the 2nd to the 13th. Center is none.

Pafnuty2.note: A Chebyshev shaper: each knob adds or subtracts one exact harmonic, from the 2nd to the 10th. Center is none. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Parametric.note: Three bands of the ConsoleX parametric EQ, the SSL-inspired bells, with frequency, gain and resonance per band. Center gain is flat.

PaulDither.note: Traditional TPDF dither with the noise highpassed so it's quieter and airier. Paul Frindle (Sony Oxford) suggested the method.

PaulWide.note: PaulDither with the left and right noise decorrelated, making it quieter, airier and wider.

PeaksOnly.note: A mix-check tool that wrecks the sound on purpose to show you what's driving your peaks. Don't master through it. No controls.

Pear.note: A testbed for Chris's Pear filter (behind his console emulations) as a high or low shelf with bit-shift-fixed cutoffs. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Pear2.note: The Pear filter with a sweepable frequency and analog-style nonlinearity.

PearEQ.note: A six-band graphic EQ built on the Pear filters from Chris's console emulations. Center is flat on each band.

PearLiteEQ.note: A four-band version of PearEQ, a secret weapon in Chris's console emulations. Center is flat on each band.

PhaseNudge.note: An allpass phase rotator like the ones radio stations use to make waveforms more symmetrical, which gives a little more headroom before limiting.

PitchDelay.note: TapeDelay2 with a fixed pitch shift in place of flutter. Each repeat shifts further up or down, and extreme down settings turn into reverse loops.

PitchNasty.note: A clean, punchy pitch shift most of the time, then audio-rate sample glitches at a pitch you set with Grind.

PlatinumSlew.note: Chris's best easy-to-use slew clipper. It tames brittle highs like an op-amp that can't quite keep up, which feels more analog than an EQ cut.

PocketVerbs.note: Chris's popular old special-effects reverbs: six types with size and a gate.

Pockey.note: Tuned for warm, fuzzy, 12-bit uLaw old-sampler texture, the lo-fi hip-hop sound.

Pockey2.note: A more efficient, more intense Pockey that can do true 4 to 16 bits.

Podcast.note: A stack of five gentle compressors with a hard clip at the end, for evening out speech.

PodcastDeluxe.note: Five compressors with phase rotators and an ADClip output, aiming at radio-station voice processing.

Point.note: An old, untameable transient shaper. Above center explodes attacks, and below center softens them.

PointyDeluxe.note: PointyGuitar's core with the gate and cab removed and ten fine EQ-plus-saturation bands exposed. It's brutal and takes over the mix, so follow it with Cabs2 or an IR. Center is neutral on every band.

PointyGuitar.note: An amp built from stacked steep EQ and saturation stages, with a resonant cab filter and a gate. You can dial in most amp types if you know the sound you're after.

Pop.note: Built to be overdriven like the little Allen & Heath limiter on 80s Phil Collins and Genesis records: huge attacks, details jumping forward, sheer exaggeration.

Pop2.note: Pop with real attack, release and drive controls. It's punchy and aggressive. Chris says it's not a hardware emulation, though he compares it to a Heritage Audio Successor.

Pop3.note: The ConsoleX dynamics: a full compressor (threshold, ratio, attack, release) and a full gate. Compressor threshold at max means off, and gate threshold at zero means off.

PowerSag.note: Models an analog circuit whose power supply can't keep up, so loud passages sag and soften, like a starved amp.

PowerSag2.note: An improved PowerSag with twice the range. Below center you hear what the sag removes.

Precious.note: A Character reissue based on Precision 8 impulses. Use it as a color adder or a fake guitar amp.

Preponderant.note: The opposite of Soothe: three tightly controlled resonant bands (narrow, medium, wide) that intensify a sound's natural resonances instead of removing them.

Pressure4.note: A golden-ear favorite. Mewiness morphs between vari-mu behavior and peak-retaining New York-style compression, and the stereo link works like a diode-bridge hardware comp.

Pressure5.note: Pressure4 plus a transient control and an output stage that can boost into a built-in ClipOnly2. Chris built it to be a whole final bus stage: compress, clip, dither, done. Turn the output down below clipping and the clipper does nothing.

Pressure6.note: The latest Pressure, refined in how it moves. Just two knobs: how much, and how far it's allowed to go.

PrimeFIR.note: A mostly linear-phase brickwall lowpass. In prime mode it leaks a strange ambience, inspired by the filter in Baconpaul's Six Sines synth.

PurestAir.note: An air-band boost or cut that refuses to boost past a set treble intensity, a bit like Air combined with Acceleration. Chris calls it an experiment.

PurestConsole2Buss.note: PurestConsole with anti-aliasing spread gently across the chain instead of a hard 20k cutoff. It keeps more top end than Console7. No controls.

PurestConsole2Channel.note: The track half of PurestConsole2. No controls.

PurestConsole3Buss.note: A minimalist Console using Chris's own sine approximation (BShifty). No controls.

PurestConsole3Channel.note: The track half of PurestConsole3. No controls.

PurestConsoleBuss.note: The least colored Console system. Just the summing interaction with nothing else. No controls.

PurestConsoleChannel.note: The track half of PurestConsole. No controls.

PurestDrive.note: An experiment that turned into a classic: very subtle, sweet saturation with a French house tone. One knob.

PurestDualPan.note: PurestGain-quality volume and pan for each channel, with fast dezippering.

PurestEcho.note: Four evenly spaced echoes, each with its own level and no feedback, so the repeats stop cleanly and don't muddy the mix. With all taps up and a very short time you get a tuned, robotic pipe tone.

PurestFade.note: PurestGain built for very long, smooth fades, made for a mastering engineer.

PurestGain.note: A high-resolution, noise-shaped gain trim with a smoothed fader.

PurestSaturation.note: A pure soft clip from a tweaked sine series, related to TapeHack. Input at 0.1 is unity.

PurestSquish.note: An open-sounding compressor with optional bass bloom, letting lows swell past the compression. It works well paired with SurgeTide.

PurestWarm.note: The softest possible saturation applied to only one half of the waveform, for subtle second-harmonic warmth.

PurestWarm2.note: PurestWarm with separate amounts for the positive and negative halves of the wave.

PurestWarm3.note: A rethought PurestWarm: one asymmetry knob for second-harmonic warmth. Center is neutral, and either side warms a different half.

Pyewacket.note: Inspired by the Pye compressors at London's Olympic Studios on 60s and 70s rock records. It sharpens transients and adds energy without fatness.

RawGlitters.note: The inverse of RawTimbers' quantization, used as a subtle brightener.

RawTimbers.note: The essence of DitherMeTimbers with no noise shaping. It's a dark, deep quantizer.

Recurve.note: A one-line compression curve with no threshold, set up for maximum explosiveness on the bus. No controls.

Remap.note: Puts the guts back into over-limited, flat audio by remapping levels to restore a sense of intensity.

ResEQ.note: Eight mostly midrange resonances to boost, Chris's answer to requests for a Soothe clone. It emphasizes sonority instead of carving it out.

ResEQ2.note: One sharp, sonorous mid peak, made for the MCI console emulation. Clearer than a plain digital bell.

RetroBass.note: A special highpass that rolls off lows in a vintage way, derived from a harmonic generator.

Reverb.note: MatrixVerb boiled down to one size knob, with everything else tuned for each size automatically. One of Chris's go-to reverbs.

Righteous4.note: A final mastering output stage: saturation aimed at a target loudness, with built-in noise shaping to 16 or 24 bit, or floating point.

RightoMono.note: Copies the right channel to both sides losslessly. No controls.

RingModulator.note: Classic ring modulation, which shifts pitches mathematically for metallic, inharmonic tones. Left and right frequencies are set separately.

SampleDelay.note: Delay in milliseconds (up to 100), whole samples (up to 10) and fractions of a sample, all combined. Use it to time-align multi-mic setups, or for comb filtering and slapback. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

Shape.note: An asymmetrical waveshaper that pulls out or squishes in parts of the waveform. Subtle peak control. Center is neutral on both knobs.

ShortBuss.note: Chases the second harmonic to add it (above center) or remove it (below center). A subtle tone-density tool. Center is neutral.

SideDull.note: A lowpass on the side channel only, which pulls treble toward the center.

Sidepass.note: A highpass on the side channel only, which mono-izes the low end.

Silhouette.note: Swaps the sound for raw noise that follows its dynamics. It's an effect, and a test of whether the groove still reads.

Silken.note: A high-frequency boost made by subtracting PrimeFIR's brickwall. It adds ambience and texture rather than plain treble.

Sinew.note: Slew clipping that gets stricter near clipping, which acts like analog tape's inability to record loud high frequencies, without the rest of the tape sound.

SingleEndedTriode.note: Unusual analog effects: single-ended triode second harmonic, plus class AB (soft) and class B (hard) crossover distortion like push-pull amps.

Slew.note: Chris's very first plugin. A slew clipper that darkens highs with a grungy, old-sampler grind. Good on hats, percussion and reverb sends. No controls.

Slew2.note: Slew with anti-aliasing added. It ended up acting like a de-esser or acceleration limiter on the very top end.

Slew3.note: A newer slew clipper aimed at a smoother, more analog darkening than Slew or Slew2.

Slew4.note: The high-frequency compression of tape without the tape. It removes digital glare and tizz only, as much as you like. One of Chris's strongest tools for harsh highs.

SlewOnly.note: A monitoring plugin that lets you hear only the extreme highs (slew). Use it to check harshness. No controls.

SlewSonic.note: Stacked SlewOnly with filtering, so you can hear only the brightness of a sound. Mainly a listening and monitoring tool.

Smooth.note: A soft clipper for spiky highs. Set gently, it butters edgy acoustics and mics. Pushed hard on drums, it makes them explode.

SmoothEQ.note: A sharp, accurate, transparent three-band EQ with steep crossovers that rebuilds the original perfectly when flat. Set it by ear like an analog EQ.

SmoothEQ2.note: A four-band shelving take on SmoothEQ with sweepable bands. Clear and intense, and Chris calls it 'wildly intuitive'. Center is flat on all knobs.

SmoothEQ3.note: The ConsoleH EQ section on its own. Chris calls it his most approachable EQ. Center is flat on each band.

SoftClock.note: A click track that leans on groove: tempo, beat count, tuplets, swing, big beat and accents, with a soft, humanized pulse.

SoftClock2.note: SoftClock with peak and valley timing shaping for a click that breathes and grooves.

SoftClock3.note: A simpler SoftClock: tempo, count, subdivision, triplets and accent flavor.

SoftGate.note: Gently fades and darkens the noise floor, made for smoothing sample tails and muting hiss. It's a slow, soft gate, not a hard one.
SoftGate.t: Soft gate for noise and tails

SpatializeDither.note: A boutique dither that's especially good at focus and reverb depth.

Spiral.note: Chris's 'smoothest possible' distortion curve, inspired by a Numberphile video. Smoother than his classic sine saturation. No controls.

Spiral2.note: Spiral with input, a highpass to keep lows clean, a presence control, output and mix.

SquareRoot.note: Soft saturation that never flat-tops: the harder you drive, the louder it keeps getting, just with more and more compression of the curve.

Srsly.note: Chris's attempt at the Hughes SRS psychoacoustic stereo processor, using narrow resonant filters to move sounds in space. He calls this first version a failure.

Srsly2.note: Srsly revisited for much more extreme widening, reverse-engineered from an old Popular Mechanics article on the Hughes SRS.

Srsly3.note: Srsly2 with a nonlinearity control that makes the filters more analog.

StarChild.note: Irregular prime-spaced echo taps loosely inspired by the Ursa Major Space Station. It makes a sci-fi digital ambience that doesn't sound like any real room.

StarChild2.note: StarChild adapted to keep its sound at high sample rates.

StereoChorus.note: A basic stereo chorus from Chris's early days. Depth scales with speed, so every setting feels about equally intense.

StereoDoubler.note: A tamed pair of GlitchShifters for detuned doubling and tripling, like a classic harmonizer double on vocals.

StereoEnsemble.note: A hyper-chorus that spreads mono or stereo sources across the field with staggered left and right delay pairs.

StereoFX.note: An aggressive stereo widener with mono bass and a center squish control.

StoneFireComp.note: ConsoleX's two-band dynamics: 'Fire' (highs) and 'Stone' (lows), split by a Kalman filter, each with its own threshold, attack, release and gain.

Stonefire.note: The ConsoleX 'non-EQ EQ': air, fire (mids/highs) and stone (lows) split by an unpredictable Kalman filter instead of fixed crossovers. Center is unity on each band.

StudioTan.note: All of Chris's 'not-a-dither' quantizers (DitherMeTimbers, RawGlitters and the like) in one plugin, updated and safe against overs.

SubTight.note: A soft slew-clipping trick from Creature, run inverted to tighten loose sub lows without a plain highpass.

SubsOnly.note: A monitoring plugin that lets you hear only the extreme lows, to check sub balance on small speakers. No controls.

Surge.note: A compressor whose ballistics make beats and pulses surge forward, adding groove rather than control.

SurgeTide.note: Three stacked compression time constants, like FM for dynamics. Chris calls it a 'sleeper' and pairs it with PurestSquish for transparent control.

Suzan.note: A new take on a ladder lowpass, a sibling of Dattorro, with a creamy synth-style resonance.

SweetWide.note: A strange, grungy experimental widener. Above center widens and below narrows. Chris warns it won't be for everyone.

Sweeten.note: One knob of super-clean second harmonic for sweetening a sound.

Swell.note: Dial in a slow attack so notes swell up after they start. It's like the pumping of kick sidechaining, but driven by the sound itself. Chris was inspired by Deadmau5's sidechain feel.

TPDFDither.note: Textbook TPDF dither: technically correct, neutral and boring by design.

TPDFWide.note: TPDF dither with decorrelated left and right noise, so it's wider and less obtrusive.

TakeCare.note: A huge, drifting chorus ensemble built on a delay matrix, inspired by The Caretaker's haunted, decaying textures. It ranges from lush to disorienting.

Tape.note: Chris's personal-favorite simple tape: Spiral-based slam plus head bump. Good on everything.

TapeBias.note: The bias part of ToTape7. Underbias gets crunchier and brighter, and overbias gets darker and softer. Center is neutral.

TapeDelay.note: One of Chris's first plugins. A tape echo with Iron Oxide-style tone shaping, and moving the time knob causes real pitch bends and dropouts.

TapeDelay2.note: A flexible modern tape echo with a band-passed feedback loop and flutter. It sounds consistent at any sample rate, and the resonance knob can get to dub-style tones.

TapeDither.note: TPDF dither with a noise spectrum like reel-to-reel tape hiss.

TapeDust.note: A 'slew noise' that erodes treble with grit, like dust and wear on tape.

TapeFat.note: The odd averaging tone control from TapeDelay. Lean subtracts it (highpass) and Fat applies it (rolls off highs, then mids).

TapeHack.note: Tape realism from hysteresis research (Spencer Walters' paper), abstracted into a soft clip. Input at 0.1 is unity.

TapeHack2.note: Two hacks combined into tape compression that Chris thinks can beat a real machine. Input at 0.1 is unity.

Texturize.note: Blends noise sculpted to the signal's brightness and dynamics underneath it, adding texture and life. Chris's honest take on 'subliminal noise' enhancers.

TexturizeMS.note: Texturize with separate settings for the mid and the sides.

Thunder.note: A compressor that keeps, or even exaggerates, subsonic bass as you push it, instead of eating low end the way most compressors do.

ToTape5.note: A classic ToTape: louder, softer, fatter (head bump) and flutter.

ToTape6.note: ToTape for 2020, bringing in UnBox, Mojo and better filtering.

ToTape7.note: The full tape machine: Dolby-style encode and decode, drive, flutter, bias and a tunable head bump. Set everything to the middle and it just works.

ToTape8.note: ToTape7 with proper gain staging and a simpler Dolby-style Tilt and Shape. Center everything for a solid default tape.

ToTape9.note: The latest ToTape, adding tape's brightness compression. Same layout as ToTape8. Center everything for a solid default.

ToVinyl4.note: Vinyl-mastering colors: separate mid and side bass highpasses (an elliptical EQ), an acceleration limiter for harsh highs, and groove wear.

ToneSlant.note: A very wide, very transparent tilt EQ. Tip the balance toward highs or lows around the middle.

TransDesk.note: Subtle analog modeling of a transistor console known for rock mixes. Chris doesn't name the desk. Punchier and edgier than Desk. No controls.

TremoSquare.note: A hard on/off tremolo that only switches at zero crossings, so it chops without clicks.

Tremolo.note: A tremolo that modulates saturation curves like a tube amp's bias tremolo, rather than plain DAW volume wobble.

Trianglizer.note: A waveshaper that bends full-scale sines toward triangles, or in the other direction to fatten.

TripleSpread.note: Splits a sound into three with the sides detuned and panned hard. Raising the mix also fades the center for a very wide image. It works on mono sources, stereo pairs or whole submixes.

Tube.note: A one-knob tube-style saturator that makes things huge. It's the seed of Chris's later analog modeling.

Tube2.note: Tube with more refined processing and an input trim.

TubeDesk.note: Subtle tube recording-console coloring: clarity and vintage character rather than mud. No controls.

Ultralight.note: The lowest-CPU matrix reverb Chris could make, built for game engines. Room settings are in steps.

Ultralight2.note: More of Ultralight. Damping at zero bypasses the reverb.

UltrasonX.note: A single ultrasonic filter stage with selectable Q. Stack several between plugins to build your own console-style anti-aliasing.

Ultrasonic.note: A clean five-stage filter that removes content above 20k so nonlinear plugins in a high-sample-rate mix alias less. It shouldn't have a sound of its own. No controls.

UltrasonicLite.note: One stage of Ultrasonic. Cheaper on CPU and gentler, so you can use many of them. No controls.

UltrasonicMed.note: Two stages of Ultrasonic. A middle ground between Lite and the full version. No controls.

UnBox.note: Distortion where only harmonics that won't alias are allowed to distort, for clean-sounding grit even at low sample rates.

VariMu.note: A more organic Pressure with vari-mu (tube compressor) behavior: the harder you hit it, the more it compresses.

VerbSevens.note: A calibrated reference reverb Chris uses to judge his 7x7 reverb matrices. No controls.

VerbSixes.note: A calibrated reference reverb using 6x6 Householder matrices. Lush and dense. No controls.

VerbThic.note: VerbTiny's sibling, voiced to be opaque and textured like classic artificial reverbs rather than a real room.

VerbTiny.note: A simple classic artificial reverb that expands a sound's shape instead of simulating a room.

Verbity.note: A dual-mono feedforward reverb that was Chris's favorite for a while: smooth, deep and natural.

Verbity2.note: Verbity with stereo cross-modulation. Chris says it may beat Galactic for deep reverbs.

Vibrato.note: A moving-delay modulator that does vibrato at full wet, chorus or flange when blended, and odd FM wobble from a second LFO. The last knob runs from inverted through dry to wet.

VinylDither.note: A high-performance dither that turns digital noise into something like vinyl groove noise, with DSD-inspired noise shaping.

VoiceOfTheStarship.note: A deep random-walk noise tone source that doesn't drift into DC. The core of Noise.

VoiceTrick.note: A trick for tracking vocals with speakers instead of headphones: mono speakers with one side flipped in polarity, so the mic hears near-cancellation. Read Chris's notes for the setup.

Weight.note: A precise sub-bass boost built on Holt filters. Chris uses it to add deep weight to live drums, DI bass or iso-cab guitars.

Wider.note: A mid/side adjuster that uses saturation density rather than plain gain: widen or narrow the sides and thicken or thin the center. Center is neutral.

Wolfbot.note: An experiment mimicking the bandpassing of the vintage Wolfbox transformer DI using two Kalman filters. The aggression comes from the filters themselves. No controls.

WoodenBox.note: A tiny box-sized reverb for giving DI instruments a wooden, acoustic-body resonance.

X2Buss.note: The ConsoleX2 bus processing, updated: a four-band EQ with sweepable frequencies, a smooth Bezier bus compressor and a fader. Center is flat on all EQ gains and frequencies.

XBandpass.note: A bandpass with distortion inside the filter, inspired by retro sampler DSP. Nuke drives the inside of the filter for zaps and grit.

XHighpass.note: A highpass with distortion inside the filter, inspired by retro sampler DSP. Nuke drives the inside of the filter for zaps and grit.

XLowpass.note: A lowpass with distortion inside the filter, inspired by retro sampler DSP. Nuke drives the inside of the filter for zaps and grit.

XNotch.note: A notch with distortion inside the filter, inspired by retro sampler DSP. Less glitchy than the other X filters.

XRegion.note: A chain of distorted bandpasses swept from a First to a Last frequency. Set them the same for a manic bandpass, or apart for extreme sound-mangling.

YBandpass.note: A bandpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal.

YHighpass.note: A highpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal.

YLowpass.note: A lowpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal.

YNotBandpass.note: A bandpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal. No control smoothing, so it's lighter on CPU but zippery if you automate it.

YNotHighpass.note: A highpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal. No control smoothing, so it's lighter on CPU but zippery if you automate it.

YNotLowpass.note: A lowpass that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal. No control smoothing, so it's lighter on CPU but zippery if you automate it.

YNotNotch.note: A notch that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal. No control smoothing, so it's lighter on CPU but zippery if you automate it.

YNotch.note: A notch that goes from soft and smooth to nasty and edgy. Resonant Edge changes the texture of the resonance, and about 0.1 is normal.

ZAcidLowpass.note: A cubic-Bezier lowpass that Chris describes as an E-mu e6400 that went insane and grew shark teeth. Built for acid squelch.

ZBandpass.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's bandpass filter, including how it distorts when driven.

ZBandpass2.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's bandpass filter, including how it distorts when driven. Adds coefficient smoothing so it moves more like the hardware when swept.

ZHighpass.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's highpass filter, including how it distorts when driven.

ZHighpass2.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's highpass filter, including how it distorts when driven. Adds coefficient smoothing so it moves more like the hardware when swept.

ZLowpass.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's lowpass filter, including how it distorts when driven.

ZLowpass2.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's lowpass filter, including how it distorts when driven. Adds coefficient smoothing so it moves more like the hardware when swept.

ZNotch.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's phaser-notch filter, including how it distorts when driven.

ZNotch2.note: Made to sound and act like the E-mu e6400 Ultra sampler's phaser-notch filter, including how it distorts when driven. Adds coefficient smoothing so it moves more like the hardware when swept.

ZOutputStage.note: The output clipping stage from Chris's E-mu e6400-style Z filters, on its own.

ZRegion.note: Staggered bandpasses from a First to a Last frequency with E-mu e6400-style hardware color.

ZRegion2.note: Staggered bandpasses from a First to a Last frequency with E-mu e6400-style hardware color. With coefficient smoothing.

Zoom.note: Stacked Density-like waveshapers that subtly move peak energy around. Above center thickens and below center opens up. Chris sees it as a possible part of a mastering plugin.

curve.note: Recurve without the extra 6 dB push or the clipper: the subtlest, purest form of the curve compressor. No controls.

kAlienSpaceship.note: A reverb found by genetic-algorithm search: realistic in behavior, unreal in size, like the inside of an alien ship.

kBeyond.note: A realistic recital hall found by genetic-algorithm search, with separate early-reflection and tail matrices.

kCathedral.note: The first of Chris's Bricasti-inspired spaces: a giant cathedral reverb with just a mix knob.

kCathedral2.note: A giant space modeled after the Bricasti M7's Cathedral program. Just a mix knob.

kCathedral3.note: A giant cathedral with Bezier undersampling and an air-compression stage, so loud sources break up like real air.

kCathedral4.note: The cathedral heard as a distant space, built on kBeyond's newer technology.

kCathedral5.note: The cathedral with a position control that places you anywhere in the room.

kChamberAR.note: Started as an attempt at the Abbey Road chamber and became a dirty, aggressive tape-echo-into-chamber sound. Lots of feedback self-oscillates and distorts.

kCosmos.note: A huge space-ambient reverb that can be a titanic hall or an endless cosmos.

kCyberCity.note: A deep reverb with a lively, urban atmosphere, built on Chris's 6x6 matrix work.

kGuitarHall.note: A hall that accentuates loud midrange, like the hockey-rink concert Chris heard as a kid. It includes air-compression loudness.

kGuitarHall2.note: A newer GuitarHall that puts things in a loud live room, with position control.

kPlate140.note: Chris's next-generation large plate reverb, the EMT 140-sized one.

kPlate240.note: The texture of a smaller gold-foil plate, the EMT 240 style. Brighter and tighter than kPlate140.

kPlateA.note: A plate in the spirit of the famous plates at Abbey Road. Chris made four (A–D), each a different plate voice.

kPlateB.note: The second Abbey Road-inspired plate, with slightly less sustain than A.

kPlateC.note: The third Abbey Road-inspired plate, a contrasting voice to B.

kPlateD.note: The last Abbey Road-inspired plate. Chris calls it a banger: the one not modified for hybrid circuitry.

kRockstar.note: A realistic hall reverb that scored highest on Chris's own realism measure and sits easily in a mix.

kRockstar2.note: kRockstar rebuilt on Chris's 'Conference' 6x6 matrix: his most impressive realistic hall.

kStation.note: A realistic small room modeled after David Bowie's vocal reverb. Small spaces like this thicken a vocal and become part of its tone instead of adding a tail.

kWoodRoom.note: A small wooden performance space. Warm, close and natural.

uLawDecode.note: The decode half of an extreme Console-like pair based on telephone uLaw companding. Put processing between uLawEncode and this for strange, intense results.

uLawEncode.note: The encode half of the uLaw pair. Follow it with your processing, then uLawDecode.
